paras: In early June 1903, notices ordering all Black residents to leave the Egypt community in Kaufman County, Texas, "under penalty of their lives" were reported posted there, signed "Mobbers." A Terrell dispatch linked the notices to the place where a white woman, Mrs. Whitworth, had been assaulted the week before, a crime for which a Black man had been hanged at Kaufman on May 30. No report of who posted the notices or whether anyone left has been found.

On May 25, 1903, dispatches from Terrell and Kaufman reported that Mrs. Whitworth, the wife of a white farmer, had been assaulted at midday by a Black man, and that armed parties were searching the countryside. That night a posse overtook a man near Kemp who broke away when questioned and was shot down; one Shreveport report said he was killed, but later Kaufman reports said he survived with serious wounds and was jailed. According to the Waxahachie Daily Light, a mob then hauled wood to the Kaufman courthouse square to burn the prisoner but was persuaded not to, and troops ordered from Dallas were recalled.

The prisoner, named in most reports as Henry Johnson, was tried on May 29, waived his appeal and his thirty days of grace, and was hanged publicly at Kaufman the next day before several thousand people, with the Terrell military company holding back the crowd. During the hanging, the Daily Light added, a Black man who lived near Kemp struck at one of Whitworth's brothers with a knife and was pursued by a crowd.

A week after the hanging, a dispatch dated Terrell, June 5, stated that "advices received in this city" told of notices posted in the Egypt community, "where the criminal assault was committed on Mrs. Whitworth last week." The notices warned "all negroes to leave that community at once under penalty of their lives" and were signed "Mobbers." The dispatch named no source, gave no date for the posting, and did not say how many notices there were or what reason they gave.
No report of departures, violence against residents, arrests, or any response by officials or by Black residents of the community appears in the coverage.

The notices reached print only as a three-sentence wire item headed "Negroes Ordered to Leave," which the Waxahachie Daily Light ran on June 5, the Bryan Morning Eagle on June 6, and the Shreveport Caucasian on June 11, each without comment. The assault case that preceded it had drawn far heavier coverage, under headlines such as "Vengeance Overtakes a Vile Negro Ravisher" and "Negro Rapist Executed." The New York Sun, under the headline "Railroaded to His Death," described the quick legal hanging as the "Nacogdoches way," said to prevent lynching and "to deter negroes from crime."
No Black-press coverage of either the notices or the Kaufman hanging was found.

Reports placed the Whitworth assault near Chief, about twenty miles south of Terrell, on the Mason farm a few miles from Kemp, or seven miles north of Kemp, and the June 5 dispatch called the spot the Egypt community; the coverage does not reconcile these names.

reader.title: Notices ordering Black residents out of the Egypt community, Kaufman County, Texas
bases: The only report of the episode describes posted notices ordering all Black residents to leave a community on threat of death; no killing, assault or completed removal is reported (A8).
All three printings carry one unattributed Terrell wire dispatch ('Advices received in this city'), with no independent or follow-up report (A8, A9, A10).

accounts.label: Terrell wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Unattributed 'advices received' in Terrell reported that notices signed "Mobbers" had been posted in the Egypt community warning all Black residents to leave at once under penalty of their lives.

framing.detail: Three papers ran the identical dispatch under the headline 'Negroes Ordered to Leave' with no comment, no named source and no follow-up.
Coverage of the preceding assault case was headed 'Vengeance Overtakes a Vile Negro Ravisher' and called the accused a 'miscreant'; the notices themselves drew no editorial line.

Posted on or before June 5, 1903 (dispatch date); exact posting date not given
No assembled mob is reported; anonymous notices were signed "Mobbers"
The same dispatch ran in three white papers (Waxahachie, Bryan, Shreveport); no Black-press coverage found
A single unattributed wire dispatch with no follow-up

record_check.dossier: Supported; the accused in that case, Henry (or John) Johnson, had been shot by a posse and was legally hanged at Kaufman on May 30, a week before the notices were reported
